analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the limitations of current preparedness strategies for Ebola viruses by highlighting the need for adaptable infrastructure that can respond to outbreaks of different viruses, including Bundibugyo virus.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a Letter published in Tropical Medicine and Health in 2026, focusing on the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the DRC and the broader context of Ebola virus preparedness.
analysis.methods: The authors analyzed operational constraints during the Bundibugyo virus outbreak, including stock-outs of Ervebo vaccine, limited team mobility, absence of vaccination microplans, shortages of personal protective equipment, and gaps in triage and isolation capacity.
analysis.main_results: The response to the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak revealed that biomedical tools alone are insufficient for outbreak control, as evidenced by temporary vaccine shortages, logistical challenges, and inadequate infrastructure.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the limitations observed during the Bundibugyo virus outbreak underscore the need for adaptable, platform-based preparedness infrastructure that integrates scientific, operational, and community readiness.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that preparedness systems must be flexible to address outbreaks of different Ebola viruses, ensuring rapid evidence generation and effective response strategies for emerging threats.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on an abstract-only analysis, which limits the depth of evidence, but the implications are grounded in the documented operational constraints during the Bundibugyo virus outbreak, supporting a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study highlights the limitations of current Ebola virus preparedness strategies, particularly in response to the 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It emphasizes that biomedical tools alone are insufficient for outbreak control, as evidenced by vaccine shortages, logistical challenges, and inadequate infrastructure. The authors propose an adaptable, platform-based approach to preparedness that integrates scientific, research, operational, and community readiness. This approach aims to enable rapid evidence generation while retaining pathogen-specific diagnostics and clinical management. The study's implications suggest that future preparedness systems must be flexible to address outbreaks of different Ebola viruses, ensuring equitable and effective action. However, the abstract-only nature of the evidence limits the depth of analysis, resulting in a moderate confidence assessment.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是 2026 年《热带医学与健康》杂志上发表的一封信,重点关注刚果民主共和国的 2026 年本迪布焦病毒病 暴发 以及 埃博拉病毒 防备的更广泛背景。

elements_zh.main_results: 对 2026 年本迪布焦病毒 暴发 的应对表明,仅靠生物医学工具不足以控制 暴发,临时 疫苗 短缺、后勤挑战和基础设施不足就证明了这一点。

abstract_zh: 刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 一直是埃博拉创新的重要场所,包括 环形疫苗接种 和基于重组水泡性口炎病毒的埃博拉 疫苗 以及临床研究与应急响应的整合。这些进展加强了对扎伊尔埃博拉病毒 (EBOV) 的防备,但 2026 年本迪布焦病毒病 (BVD) 暴发 凸显了一个剩余的局限性:许多防备能力仍然与个体病原体密切相关。与 EBOV 不同,本迪布焦病毒 (BDBV) 没有获得专门用于预防的许可 疫苗,并且目前的证据不足以建立 Ervebo 对人类 BVD 具有临床意义的保护作用。当前应对措施中记录的操作限制,包括临时 Ervebo 缺货、疫苗接种 团队流动性有限、缺乏 疫苗接种 微观计划、个人防护设备短缺以及下韦莱省分诊和隔离能力的差距,进一步说明仅靠生物医学工具无法确保有效的 疫苗接种 控制。我们建议通过适应性强、基于平台的 暴发 基础设施来扩展针对病原体的准备工作,该基础设施涵盖四个相关领域:科学准备、研究和监管准备、操作准备和社区准备。此类平台应能够快速生成证据,同时保留病原体特异性诊断、临床管理、疫苗 和流行病学知识。因此,在 传播 超过应对能力之前,全球准备工作应支持从不确定性向证据和公平行动的转变。

title: Revisiting the phylogeny of African Pteropodidae (Chiroptera) known to potentially host Filoviridae viruses
abstract: Abstract Recent global changes, largely driven mostly by human activities, have increased the frequency and intensity of contacts between humans and wildlife, leading to the emergence of new zoonotic diseases at human/wildlife interfaces. Within the framework of the One Health paradigm, a comprehensive understanding of the ecology of host species involved in multi-host pathogen dynamics is essential. This understanding can be enhanced through the study of these dynamics within individual hosts and across different host species. Establishing evolutionary relationships through accurate and robust phylogenetic analyses, combined with the ecological characteristics of the species can help to predict possible new host species. Chiropterans have been identified as significant reservoirs for various zoonotic pathogens, predominantly viruses. In Africa, species within the Pteropodidae family (Old World Fruit Bat) have been identified as potential maintenance hosts of the Filoviridae viruses including Ebola and Marburg virus, which present a public health importance. Our study refines African Pteropodidae phylogenies by incorporating multiple specimens per species, adding 20 new mitochondrial genome sequences, and integrating sequences of five nuclear markers (BRCA1, FGB, RAG1, RAG2, vWF) from 33 specimens. These additions reduce phylogenetic artefacts and provide a comprehensive view of African Pteropodidae evolutionary history.

source_records.title: Revisiting the phylogeny of African Pteropodidae (Chiroptera) known to potentially host Filoviridae viruses
source_records.abstract: Abstract Recent global changes, largely driven mostly by human activities, have increased the frequency and intensity of contacts between humans and wildlife, leading to the emergence of new zoonotic diseases at human/wildlife interfaces. Within the framework of the One Health paradigm, a comprehensive understanding of the ecology of host species involved in multi-host pathogen dynamics is essential. This understanding can be enhanced through the study of these dynamics within individual hosts and across different host species. Establishing evolutionary relationships through accurate and robust phylogenetic analyses, combined with the ecological characteristics of the species can help to predict possible new host species. Chiropterans have been identified as significant reservoirs for various zoonotic pathogens, predominantly viruses. In Africa, species within the Pteropodidae family (Old World Fruit Bat) have been identified as potential maintenance hosts of the Filoviridae viruses including Ebola and Marburg virus, which present a public health importance. Our study refines African Pteropodidae phylogenies by incorporating multiple specimens per species, adding 20 new mitochondrial genome sequences, and integrating sequences of five nuclear markers (BRCA1, FGB, RAG1, RAG2, vWF) from 33 specimens. These additions reduce phylogenetic artefacts and provide a comprehensive view of African Pteropodidae evolutionary history.

title: Tribute: Dr. Charles Mbusa Munyumu – killed in action for neurosurgery
abstract: On August 10, 2026, Dr. Charles Mbusa Munyumu died of Ebola virus disease in Butembo, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo. He had contracted Bundibugyo virus while operating on a patient. He was 48, had qualified in neurosurgery in Dakar, and had returned home only months earlier. He was the antithesis of the brain drain: He acquired a rare skill abroad and deliberately brought it back to a population with almost no access to neurosurgical care, in a region marked by decades of armed conflict and recurrent epidemics. This tribute records his life and the circumstances of his death, and calls for concrete support to African neurosurgery: Training, equipment, sustained partnerships, and protection for health professionals working in areas of conflict and epidemic.

title: Preparation of Excipient-Free Molnupiravir Microparticles for Pulmonary Drug Delivery and Process Evaluation via Machine Learning
abstract: Background/Objective: Molnupiravir (EIDD-2801) was originally designed to treat influenza A virus and showed broad-spectrum antiviral activity, including against influenza virus, Ebola virus, coronavirus and other viruses. Methods: In this study, molnupiravir microparticles were firstly prepared by spray freeze-drying (SFD) and jet milling (JM) methods. Meanwhile, machine learning methodology was applied to evaluate the influence of process parameters such as feeding rate, concentration, and nebulization pressure on powder properties. Results: According to SEM images, the microparticles prepared by SFD presented a porous and near-spherical structure. Moreover, the fine particle fraction (FPF) and mass median aerodynamic diameter (MMAD) of the optimal inhalable powder reached up to 70.19 ± 2.06% and 2.80 ± 0.16 μm, proving the excellent aerodynamic performance. Conclusions: The molnupiravir micropowder showed preliminary short-term storage behavior after storage for 28 days at 25 °C and 60% RH.

Methods: In this study, molnupiravir microparticles were firstly prepared by spray freeze-drying (SFD) and jet milling (JM) methods. Meanwhile, machine learning methodology was applied to evaluate the influence of process parameters such as feeding rate, concentration, and nebulization pressure on powder properties. Results: According to SEM images, the microparticles prepared by SFD presented a porous and near-spherical structure. Moreover, the fine particle fraction (FPF) and mass median aerodynamic diameter (MMAD) of the optimal inhalable powder reached up to 70.19 ± 2.06% and 2.80 ± 0.16 μm, proving the excellent aerodynamic performance. Conclusions: The molnupiravir micropowder showed preliminary short-term storage behavior after storage for 28 days at 25 °C and 60% RH.

analysis.summary_en: This study focuses on the preparation of excipient-free molnupiravir microparticles for pulmonary drug delivery and evaluates their properties using machine learning. The background highlights molnupiravir's broad-spectrum antiviral activity, including against Ebola virus. The methods involved spray freeze-drying and jet milling to create microparticles, with machine learning used to analyze the effects of process parameters on powder properties. title: Improving the Resolution and Informativity of the Majority-Rule Consensus Tree Using Fine-Grained Dissimilarity Measures
abstract: Phylogenetic analyses often require the summarization of multiple trees, e.g., in Bayesian analyses to obtain the centroid of the posterior distribution of trees, or to determine the consensus of a set of bootstrap trees. The majority-rule consensus tree is the most commonly used. It is easy to compute and minimizes the sum of Robinson-Foulds (RF) distances to the input trees. In mathematical terms, the majority-rule consensus tree is the median of the input trees with respect to the RF distance. However, due to the coarse nature of RF distance, which only considers whether two branches induce exactly the same bipartition of the taxa or not, highly unresolved trees can be produced when the phylogenetic signal is low. To overcome this limitation, we propose using median trees with respect to finer-grained dissimilarity measures between trees. These measures include a quartet distance between tree topologies, and transfer distances, which quantify the similarity between bipartitions, in contrast to the presence/absence view of RF. We describe fast heuristic consensus algorithms for transfer-based tree dissimilarities, capable of efficiently processing trees with thousands of taxa. Through evaluations on simulated datasets in both Bayesian and bootstrapping maximum-likelihood frameworks, our results show that our methods improve consensus tree resolution in scenarios with low to moderate phylogenetic signal, while providing better or comparable dissimilarities to the true phylogeny. Applying our methods to mammals, Ebola virus, and a large HIV dataset of over nine thousand taxa confirms the improvement with real data. These results demonstrate the usefulness of our new consensus tree methods for analyzing the large datasets that are available today. Our software, PhyloCRISP, is available from https://github.com/yukiregista/PhyloCRISP.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Phylogenetic analyses often require the summarization of multiple trees, e.g., in Bayesian analyses to obtain the centroid of the posterior distribution of trees, or to determine the consensus of a set of bootstrap trees. The majority-rule consensus tree is the most commonly used.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study describes a computational approach to improve consensus tree resolution using fine-grained dissimilarity measures. It evaluates the method on simulated datasets and real-world data including mammals, Ebola virus, and a large HIV dataset of over nine thousand taxa.
analysis.methods: The methods involve developing fast heuristic consensus algorithms for transfer-based tree dissimilarities, which quantify the similarity between bipartitions rather than using the coarse Robinson-Foulds (RF) distance. These algorithms are designed to efficiently process trees with thousands of taxa.
analysis.main_results: Through evaluations on simulated datasets in both Bayesian and bootstrapping maximum-likelihood frameworks, the results show that the proposed methods improve consensus tree resolution in scenarios with low to moderate phylogenetic signal, while providing better or comparable dissimilarities to the true phylogeny. Applying the methods to real data confirms the improvement.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that their new consensus tree methods are more informative and better suited for analyzing large datasets with low to moderate phylogenetic signal. The novelty lies in the use of fine-grained dissimilarity measures that capture more detailed relationships between bipartitions.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the analysis of large phylogenetic datasets, particularly those involving human-pathogenic orthoebolaviruses, by providing more accurate and resolved consensus trees. This has implications for understanding viral evolution and improving outbreak response.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to simulated and real datasets, and the effectiveness of the methods may depend on the quality and quantity of the input data. The evidence strength is moderate, as the results are based on computational evaluations rather than clinical or epidemiological outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a new method for improving the resolution and informativity of consensus trees in phylogenetic analyses by using fine-grained dissimilarity measures instead of the traditional Robinson-Foulds (RF) distance. The majority-rule consensus tree, commonly used in Bayesian and bootstrapping analyses, is known to produce highly unresolved trees when phylogenetic signal is low. The proposed method employs quartet distances and transfer distances to better capture the similarity between bipartitions. Evaluations on simulated datasets and real-world data, including Ebola virus and HIV datasets, demonstrate that the new approach enhances consensus tree resolution in low to moderate signal scenarios. The study highlights the importance of these methods for analyzing large datasets, particularly those involving human-pathogenic orthoebolaviruses, and suggests their potential utility in understanding viral evolution and improving outbreak response. The evidence is based on computational performance and is considered moderate in strength due to the absence of direct clinical or epidemiological outcomes.

title_zh: 使用细粒度相异性度量提高多数规则共识树的分辨率和信息量
source_body_en: Phylogenetic analyses often require the summarization of multiple trees, e.g., in Bayesian analyses to obtain the centroid of the posterior distribution of trees, or to determine the consensus of a set of bootstrap trees. The majority-rule consensus tree is the most commonly used. It is easy to compute and minimizes the sum of Robinson-Foulds (RF) distances to the input trees. In mathematical terms, the majority-rule consensus tree is the median of the input trees with respect to the RF distance. However, due to the coarse nature of RF distance, which only considers whether two branches induce exactly the same bipartition of the taxa or not, highly unresolved trees can be produced when the phylogenetic signal is low. To overcome this limitation, we propose using median trees with respect to finer-grained dissimilarity measures between trees. These measures include a quartet distance between tree topologies, and transfer distances, which quantify the similarity between bipartitions, in contrast to the presence/absence view of RF. We describe fast heuristic consensus algorithms for transfer-based tree dissimilarities, capable of efficiently processing trees with thousands of taxa. Through evaluations on simulated datasets in both Bayesian and bootstrapping maximum-likelihood frameworks, our results show that our methods improve consensus tree resolution in scenarios with low to moderate phylogenetic signal, while providing better or comparable dissimilarities to the true phylogeny. Applying our methods to mammals, Ebola virus, and a large HIV dataset of over nine thousand taxa confirms the improvement with real data. These results demonstrate the usefulness of our new consensus tree methods for analyzing the large datasets that are available today. Our software, PhyloCRISP, is available from https://github.com/yukiregista/PhyloCRISP.
abstract_zh: 系统发育分析通常需要对多个树进行汇总,例如,在贝叶斯分析中以获得树后验分布的质心,或确定一组引导树的共识。多数规则共识树是最常用的。它很容易计算并最小化到输入树的 Robinson-Foulds (RF) 距离之和。用数学术语来说,多数规则共识树是输入树相对于 RF 距离的中值。然而,由于RF距离的粗略性质,仅考虑两个分支是否引起完全相同的类群二分,当系统发育信号较低时,可能会产生高度未解析的树。为了克服这一限制,我们建议使用中值树来实现树之间更细粒度的相异性度量。这些度量包括树拓扑之间的四重距离和传输距离,它们量化了二分区之间的相似性,与 RF 的存在/不存在视图形成对比。我们描述了基于转移的树差异的快速启发式共识算法,能够有效地处理具有数千个类群的树。通过对贝叶斯和引导最大似然框架中的模拟数据集进行评估,我们的结果表明,我们的方法在具有低到中等系统发育信号的情况下提高了共识树分辨率,同时提供了与真实 系统发育 更好或相当的差异。将我们的方法应用于哺乳动物、埃博拉病毒 和超过 9000 个分类单元的大型 HIV 数据集,证实了真实数据的改进。这些结果证明了我们新的共识树方法在分析当今可用的大型数据集方面的有用性。我们的软件 PhyloCRISP 可从 https://github.com/yukiregista/PhyloCRISP 获取。
